Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you get started, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a remote repository, inspect its files, or run `git` commands from here. What I *can* do is generate the two artifacts you asked for (a Dockerfile and a Kubernetes deployment/service) using the helper functions that were supplied, and then give you a ready‑to‑paste GitHub Actions workflow that you can drop into the repo yourself.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can follow locally:

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re not already authenticated with SSH keys, you’ll need to set those up first (`ssh-keygen`, add public key to GitHub, etc.).

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Assuming the repo is a standard Node.js project that runs `node app.js` (or whatever entry point it uses), we’ll generate a minimal Dockerfile that installs dependencies and starts the app.

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "node app.js"
}
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small and fast, and Node 18 is LTS at the time of writing. Adjust the tag if your app requires a different Node version.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes Deployment & Service

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP"
}
```

> **What this does**  
> - Creates a deployment named `nodejs-welcome` that pulls the image you’ll build/push later.  
> - Exposes 3 replicas so the app is highly available.  
> - Sets up a `ClusterIP` service (internal load balancer). Change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

> **Note** – Replace `"your-dockerhub-username"` with your actual Docker Hub username (or another registry).

---

## 3️⃣ Add Generated Files to Git

After running the two function calls above, you’ll end up with:

- `Dockerfile`
- `kubernetes.yaml` (or separate `deployment.yaml` + `service.yaml`)

Add them to the repo:

```bash
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml
```

If you prefer separate files, adjust the names accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests"
git push origin main
```

---

## 5️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow (Manual Step)

Create a new file `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (replace with your registry if needed)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Tag the image as latest
      - name: Tag as latest
        run: |
          docker tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
                     ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

### Setting Up Secrets

In your GitHub repo settings → **Secrets & variables → Actions**, add:

| Secret Name | Value |
|-------------|-------|
| `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username |
| `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub personal access token (with “write” permissions) |

> **Why a token?**  
> Tokens are more secure than passwords and can be scoped to specific repos.

---

## 6️⃣ Deploy to Kubernetes (Optional)

Once the image is pushed, you can apply the manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f kubernetes.yaml
```

Or split into two files:

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
```

---

## Summary

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Clone repo locally |
| 2 | Run the two helper functions to generate Dockerfile & Kubernetes YAML |
| 3 | Add generated files to git |
| 4 | Commit & push |
| 5 | Manually create GitHub Actions workflow (as shown) |
| 6 | (Optional) Apply Kubernetes manifests |

Feel free to tweak the generated Dockerfile or Kubernetes YAML to match any special requirements your app has (e.g., environment variables, volume mounts, health checks, etc.). Once you’ve committed everything, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and push a new image whenever you push to `main`.
